Following the 2008 presidential election, voters held significantly more positive expectations and expressed a stronger desire for political leaders to cooperate compared to the aftermath of the 2016 election. 

In November 2008, 74% of all voters believed Republican leaders should work with President Barack Obama, whereas only 22% felt they should stand up to him ![A survey showing voter opinions from 2008 and 2016 on working with versus standing up to newly elected presidents](image1). Even among Republicans and Republican leaners in 2008, nearly six-in-ten (59%) advocated for GOP leaders to work with Obama [1]. By contrast, in November 2016, only 59% of all voters thought Democratic leaders should work with Donald Trump, while 39% wanted them to stand up to him ![A survey showing voter opinions from 2008 and 2016 on working with versus standing up to newly elected presidents](image1). Furthermore, 65% of Democrats wanted their leaders to stand up to Trump, with only 32% supporting cooperation ![A survey showing voter opinions from 2008 and 2016 on working with versus standing up to newly elected presidents](image1).

General sentiments and expectations of success were similarly higher in 2008. Following Obama's election, 58% of voters reported feeling happy with the outcome [3], and 67% expected his term to be successful ![A bar chart comparing expectations of presidential success for Trump in 2016 and Obama in 2008](image2). In 2016, only 50% of voters were happy with Trump's election [3], and a smaller majority of 56% anticipated a successful term ![A bar chart comparing expectations of presidential success for Trump in 2016 and Obama in 2008](image2). Expectations among supporters of losing candidates were also markedly lower in 2016; while 39% of John McCain supporters in 2008 expected Obama to have a successful first term, only 15% of Hillary Clinton supporters in 2016 thought Trump's first term would be successful [4].

In summary, voters in 2008 demonstrated greater optimism and significantly higher support for political cooperation with the incoming president than voters did in 2016.

Based on the provided evaluation results, the model that achieves the highest F1-value for Named Entity Recognition (NER) is **CCNN+WLSTM+CRF**, attaining an F1 score of 91.35 ![The performance table shows that CCNN+WLSTM+CRF achieves the highest F1 score of 91.35 in NER.](image1).

Several architectural components and feature types contribute to this performance:

- **Word-Level and Inference Layer Baseline**: The architecture relies on a word-level Long Short-Term Memory network paired with Conditional Random Fields (`WLSTM+CRF`) as its core sequence labeling framework [1], [3].
- **Human-Engineered Features**: Features such as Part-of-Speech tags (`+POS`) and capitalization indicators (`+Cap`) provide helpful contextual signals when converted into dense lookup embeddings [3]. 
- **Automatic Character-Level Features**: The most critical performance boost comes from automatically encoding character sequence information using a Character CNN (`+CCNN`) or Character LSTM (`+CLSTM`) ![The feature comparison table indicates that adding CCNN features improves the NER F1 score to 91.35, outperforming human-engineered features.](image3). Automatically learning character-level representations captures intra-word structures and morphological patterns far more effectively than relying strictly on manual features [3].

The CCNN+WLSTM+CRF model achieves the highest F1-value for NER, driven by combining automatic character-level CNN representations with word-level LSTM context and CRF sequence decoding.

In machine translation evaluation, direct assessment (DA) scores assigned by human annotators are converted into pairwise quality comparisons ($daRR$) [1][2]. To accomplish this, input source sentences receiving DA scores for at least two distinct translations ($DA > 1$) are collected to form translation pairs [1]. The metric $Ave$ measures the average number of translations with at least one DA judgment available per source sentence, while $daRR$ represents the total number of pairwise comparisons remaining after excluding human ties and small score differences of 25 percentage points or less [1][4].

![Table 1 details the DA>1, Ave, DA pairs, and daRR statistics across different language pairs.](image1)

The resulting pairwise human evaluation metrics ($daRR$) vary significantly across language pairs depending on the dataset size and the number of available candidate translations [2]. For instance, among translation directions into English, German-to-English (`de-en`) yields the largest overall volume of pairwise human evaluations with $n = 85,365$ $daRR$ judgments [2].

![The table highlights human evaluation scores and sample sizes (n) across language pairs to English.](image2)

Conversely, language pairs such as German–French (`de-fr`) and French–German (`fr-de`) have substantially fewer available comparisons, with $daRR$ sample sizes of $n = 4,862$ and $n = 1,369$ respectively [2].

![The table provides human evaluation sample sizes (n) for German-Czech, German-French, and French-German pairs.](image3)

Table 1 records the average number of DA-judged translations ($Ave$) and the corresponding $daRR$ count for each language pair, with German-to-English (`de-en`) having the highest number of pairwise assessments ($daRR = 85,365$).

Nuclear DNA repair mechanisms encompass several specialized pathways designed to address mutations based on the specific type, site, and extent of the damage [1]. 

![Figure 11 demonstrates various DNA repair mechanisms including Base Excision Repair, Mismatch Repair, Nucleotide Excision Repair, and Recombinational repair in response to specific types of DNA damage.](image1)

As illustrated in Figure 11, the key DNA repair mechanisms demonstrated include:

- **Base Excision Repair (BER)**: Addresses single-base mutations, 8-Oxoguanine, and single-strand breaks (SSB) caused by agents like oxygen radicals and alkylating agents [1].
- **Mismatch Repair (MMR)**: Corrects single base mismatches as well as insertions and deletions arising from replication errors [1].
- **Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER)**: Repairs pyrimidine dimers and bulky adducts induced by factors such as UV light [1, 3].
- **Recombinational Repair (Recombination Repair)**: Repairs severe lesions like double-strand breaks (DSB) and interstrand cross-links caused by DNA damaging drugs or radiation, utilizing pathways such as homologous recombination [1, 4].

In conclusion, Figure 11 demonstrates Base Excision Repair (BER), Mismatch Repair (MMR), Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER), and Recombinational repair [1].

A neural network model combines both word-level and character-level embeddings to capture distinct aspects of language representations:

* **Character-level embeddings**: A character-level neural network (such as a Bi-LSTM, RNN, or CNN) processes character sequences to capture subword information, including morphological variations and capitalization patterns [3]. 
* **Word-level embeddings**: These vectors capture the broader semantic representations and contextual meaning of individual words within a vector space.

![A Self-attentive Bi-LSTM-CRF model architecture concatenates character and word embeddings to feed into a word-level Bi-LSTM layer.](image1)

By concatenating each word's character-level representation with its corresponding word embedding, the architecture produces a comprehensive input vector for the word-level network (such as a Bi-LSTM) [2]. This dual input enables the model to effectively leverage overall semantic meanings while maintaining sensitivity to fine-grained subword features and morphological nuances [2, 3].

In summary, a model uses both word-level and character-level embeddings to simultaneously capture broad semantic context and fine-grained subword details such as morphology and capitalization patterns.

In DETR object detection models, positional encodings—encompassing spatial encodings for image features as well as learned output encodings for object queries—play a fundamental role in maintaining high Average Precision (AP) [2, 4]. 

Completely removing spatial positional encodings results in a severe performance drop of 7.8 AP relative to the baseline, though the model still manages to achieve over 32 AP [1, 2]. 

![The table demonstrates that completely omitting spatial positional encodings causes a severe drop in AP, whereas including them across encoder and decoder attention layers yields the highest performance.](image1)

When fixed sine spatial positional encodings are passed only once at the input—akin to the original transformer architecture—the model experiences a 1.4 AP drop compared to supplying positional encodings directly at every attention layer [2]. Interestingly, excluding spatial encodings strictly from the encoder leads to only a minor AP drop of 1.3 to 1.4 AP, indicating that spatial encodings within the decoder are particularly key for accurate predictions [1, 2]. Furthermore, output positional encodings (object queries) are indispensable and must be provided either at the decoder input or continuously added to queries at every decoder attention layer [2]. Overall, transformer components including spatial and output positional encodings, global self-attention, FFNs, and decoder layers all significantly contribute to maximizing object detection performance [4].

Positional encoding configurations strongly influence Average Precision, where entirely omitting spatial positional encodings causes a drastic drop in AP, while passing spatial encodings directly into all attention layers produces the highest AP.

The study of computational detection of diachronic semantic shifts advanced rapidly between 2010 and 2017, marked by key technical innovations, methodological refinements, and the introduction of diverse historical and temporal corpora [2].

![The timeline illustrates key developments in diachronic semantic shift research from 2010 to 2017.](image1)

The progression of milestones during this period developed as follows:

* **2010**: The field adopted the concept of a "Time tensor with Random Indexing", allowing semantic vectors for words to be quantitatively tracked across sequential time spans [4].
* **2011**: Researchers began utilizing large-scale diachronic datasets, prominently featuring the Google Ngrams corpus [1].
* **2012**: Work focused on refined temporal disambiguation techniques, such as "Word epoch disambiguation".
* **2013**: The field shifted toward prediction-based models to represent word meanings continuously over time [2].
* **2014**: The introduction and widespread implementation of prediction-based "Word embeddings" (such as word2vec) revolutionized semantic vector representations.
* **2015**: Important progress was made in "Models alignment" to align distinct vector spaces across temporal slices, alongside the use of shorter time-granularity datasets like Amazon Movie Reviews and Twitter [1].
* **2016**: Corpus diversity broadened significantly to include long-term historical and news archives, notably the New York Times Annotated Corpus ("NYT corpus") and the Corpus of Historical American English ("COHA corpus") [1].
* **2017**: The field achieved major analytical breakthroughs, including "Joint learning across time spans", the application of the "Gigaword corpus" [1], investigation into "Diachronic relations" [3], as well as the statistical formulation and criticism of the "Laws of semantic change" [3].

In summary, the key milestones from 2010 to 2017 span the development of time tensors, prediction-based embeddings, vector alignment, joint learning, and the integration of major historical corpora like Google Ngrams, COHA, NYT, and Gigaword.

In the provided example annotation of a text passage concerning *Super Mario Land*, entities and their relationships are represented through a structured breakdown that maps individual tokens to variables corresponding to the generative process of a Knowledge Graph Language Model (KGLM) [1]. 

![This table shows the structured breakdown of the passage into tokens, mention types, entities, relations, and parent entities.](image1)

The representation includes five primary attributes for each token [1]:

* **Tokens ($x_t$)**: Individual words or spans of text within the passage (e.g., "1989", "Nintendo", or "Game Boy") [1].
* **Mention Type ($t_t$)**: Classifies how an entity mention is introduced, such as designating it as a "new" entity or a "related" entity based on whether it is reachable from entities previously linked in the discourse [1].
* **Entity Mentioned ($e_t$)**: Links specific text tokens to their corresponding Wikidata entity or value (such as linking "1989" to `04-21-1989` or "Nintendo" to `NIN`) [1].
* **Relation ($r_t$)**: Defines the specific relationship connecting entities, such as `pub date` for publication date or `genre` for video game genre [1].
* **Parent Entity ($p_t$)**: Identifies the context or origin entity connected to the target entity through the specified relation; for example, "SML" (Super Mario Land) serves as the parent entity for its publication date and genre [1].

In addition, distinct entities are color-coded in the annotation table to clearly differentiate entity types and trace their interconnected relationships across the passage [1].

In summary, entities and their relationships in the example annotation are represented by mapping each text token to a mention type ($t_t$), a target entity ($e_t$), a relation ($r_t$), and a parent entity ($p_t$).

The evaluation of confidence and likelihood levels is grounded in expert assessment and consensus among author teams [1, 4]. To determine these levels, authors systematically review the available literature, assess the quality, quantity, and consistency of evidence, and gauge the level of agreement across different studies [1, 2].

Confidence is expressed qualitatively, reflecting the strength and validity of a finding based on the available evidence and expert consensus [2]. It spans four distinct levels ranging from low confidence (inconclusive evidence or expert disagreement) up to very high confidence (strong evidence, consistent results, and high consensus) [2].

![The chart categorizes confidence levels from low to very high based on evidence strength, methods, and expert consensus.](image1)

In contrast, likelihood language describes the probability of a specific outcome or impact occurring [1, 2]. It translates subjective assessments into defined probability terms with clear numerical ranges, spanning from "Very Unlikely" ($\le$ 1 in 10) to "Very Likely" ($\ge$ 9 in 10) [2].

![The image defines likelihood levels using probability terms ranging from 'Very Unlikely' (less than or equal to 1 in 10) to 'Very Likely' (greater than or equal to 9 in 10).](image2)

 levels of confidence and likelihood are evaluated through expert consensus assessing the quality and consistency of evidence qualitatively alongside standardized numerical probability ranges for likelihood terms.

In Belize, the legal landscape regarding defamation and blasphemy was updated through the modernizing of its statutory framework [1]. 

![Section 18 of the Defamation Act, 2022 replaced the revised Libel and Defamation Act of 2020 in Belize, defining media privilege rules while remaining rarely enforced.](image1)

Specifically, Belize enacted the Defamation Act, 2022 (No. 15 of 2022), which replaced the earlier Libel and Defamation Act, Chapter 169 (revised laws of Belize 2020). Under Section 18 of the 2022 Act, the law establishes specific parameters governing news media, granting privilege to certain publications unless malice is proven. However, it explicitly excludes illegal publications or matters that are not of public interest. Furthermore, according to the U.S. State Department’s 2022 Report on International Religious Freedom, these provisions are rarely enforced in practice.

In summary, Belize updated its legal landscape by replacing its 2020 Libel and Defamation Act with the Defamation Act of 2022 to outline media privilege protections, though the law is rarely enforced.

On the GLUE benchmark, BERT models generally outperform CNN models across overall average performance scores as well as individual tasks ![BERT_LARGE and BERT_BASE achieve superior average scores and strong performance across GLUE tasks compared to CNN models.](image2). While CNN models demonstrate competitive baseline capabilities—with larger variants like CNN Large showing clear gains over CNN Base [1]—their performance lags behind BERT, particularly on complex sentence-pair tasks [1, 2]. 

Specifically, on sentence-pair evaluation tasks such as MRPC and RTE, BERT models show a significant performance advantage compared to CNN architectures [1]. This difference stems from architectural and pre-training differences: while bidirectional CNN models optimize single-token prediction given surrounding context [1, 4], BERT leverages full bidirectional self-attention and pre-training objectives like next sentence prediction [4], making it substantially stronger at capturing relationships across sentence pairs [1, 4].

In conclusion, BERT models outperform CNN models on the GLUE benchmark overall, demonstrating superior strength in understanding sentence-pair relationships due to their full bidirectional context and multi-task pre-training objectives.

The Bi-LSTM Utterance Encoder (also referred to as the utterance-level LSTM) serves to process and convert the user's natural language input into a continuous vector representation [1, 2]. 

When a user provides input in natural language format, the words are first mapped into an embedding space and then fed step-by-step into a bidirectional LSTM [2]. The encoder processes the sequence in both forward and backward directions, concatenating the final forward state ($\overrightarrow{h_{T_k}}$) and backward state ($\overleftarrow{h_1}$) to generate the final user utterance vector ($U_k$) at turn $k$ [2].

![The Bi-LSTM Utterance Encoder converts natural language user input into an utterance vector, which is fed into the dialogue-level LSTM.](image1)

This continuous user utterance encoding, combined with the continuous representation of the previous system action, is directly passed as an input into the dialogue-level LSTM ($\mathrm{LSTM_D}$) [1, 4]. This enables the system to continuously update and maintain the dialogue state across conversation turns [1, 4].

The function of the Bi-LSTM Utterance Encoder is to encode natural language user input into a continuous vector representation that serves as an input to update the dialogue state.

The **Post-hoc Correction with External Feedback** strategy refines generated model outputs by integrating feedback from both a critic model and specialized external tools [1]. 

In post-hoc correction methods, refinement takes place after the complete output has been produced by the language model, operating without updating the underlying model parameters [2]. This framework allows for more flexible and transparent natural language feedback [2].

![Post-hoc Correction with External Feedback leverages critic model reviews and external tools like search engines, code interpreters, and knowledge bases to refine outputs after generation.](image1)

Specifically, under the **Post-hoc Correction with External Feedback** workflow, the process unfolds through the following steps:
1. **Initial Generation**: The core language model produces the initial outputs [1].
2. **Critic Review**: A critic model evaluates the output and provides diagnostic feedback or natural language suggestions [1].
3. **External Assistance**: Rather than relying purely on the base language model's internal capabilities, external models and tools—such as search engines, knowledge bases, trained domain models, and code interpreters—are brought in to assist and guide the refinement cycle.

By bringing external resources into the feedback loop, this strategy helps overcome the limitations of pure self-correction, which often falters or requires massive model scale to perform effective self-refinement [4].

In conclusion, the 'Post-hoc Correction with External Feedback' strategy enhances output refinement by integrating external tools such as knowledge bases, search engines, and code interpreters with critic feedback to correct and refine generated text.

Hamilton County, located in east-central Nebraska, experienced dramatic demographic shifts between 1870 and 2000 ![A map of Hamilton County, Nebraska highlighting its main communities and road network.](image1). 

In 1870, the census recorded a sparse population of just 130 residents in the county [2]. As pioneer overland travel intensified and the expanding railroad system captured freight traffic, settlement surged rapidly during the late 19th century [2]. Consequently, the population exploded to 8,267 by 1880 and reached an all-time peak of 14,096 residents in 1890 [2].

Following this peak, Hamilton County's population began a slow, continuous decline over the next several decades [2]. By the mid-20th century, the county's population dropped to 8,778 in 1950 and 8,714 in 1960 ![A table recording the total census population of Hamilton County from 1870 to 2000.](image2). This contraction was largely driven by agricultural shifts such as farm consolidation, which led five of the seven rural communities in the county to reach their population peaks between 1900 and 1940 before declining [1]. 

During the late 20th century, the county's population stabilized around 8,800 to 9,400, reaching 9,403 by the 2000 census (image2). This stabilization was significantly supported by growth in specific local hubs; notably, Aurora experienced a steady rise in population from 1940 onward, peaking at 4,225 citizens in 2000 and counteracting the broader trend of rural decline in smaller surrounding towns [1].

In summary, Hamilton County's population rapidly surged from 130 in 1870 to a peak of 14,096 in 1890 due to pioneer settlement and railroad expansion, before declining and eventually stabilizing at 9,403 by 2000 as a result of farm consolidation and centralized town growth in Aurora.

* **Commonsense knowledge**: 5.3%

### Relation to Reasoning Complexity

This diverse composition of atomic operations directly drives the complexity and depth of the reasoning process required for claim verification [1, 4]. Because verifying a scientific claim typically requires chaining multiple operations—such as retrieving contextual background knowledge from captions (closed-domain knowledge), retrieving values (simple lookup), and performing numerical math or comparisons—the claims demand multi-step reasoning [1, 4].

![The histogram depicts the distribution of reasoning steps in SciTab, demonstrating that 86% of claims require 3 or more steps.](image1)

As a result of combining these varied reasoning functions, 86% of the claims in SciTab require 3 or more reasoning steps, with an average reasoning depth of 4.76 steps and a maximum depth reaching up to 11 steps [1].

Compared to existing multimodal datasets that focus primarily on daily commonsense and simple physical or temporal reasoning, the MMMU benchmark extends both knowledge breadth and reasoning depth to a college level [1, 4]. In terms of breadth, MMMU spans college-level subjects across 183 subfields, whereas previous benchmarks cover limited everyday domains [1, 4]. In terms of depth, it requires deliberate expert reasoning—such as applying domain-specific concepts like the Fourier Transform or Equilibrium Theory—rather than surface-level perception [1, 4].

![MMMU excels in both reasoning depth and knowledge breadth compared to previous multimodal benchmarks like VQA, GQA, and VisWiz.](image1)

The dataset contains a total of 11.5K multimodal questions sourced from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, partitioned into a few-shot development set, a validation set of ~900 questions, and a test set of 10.5K questions [3, 4]. These questions are distributed across six major college disciplines: Engineering (26%), Science (23%), Health & Medicine (17%), Business (14%), Art & Design (11%), and Humanities & Social Sciences (9%) [4]. 

![The MMMU benchmark covers six primary college disciplines while challenging LMMs with expert-level visual perception, domain knowledge, and complex reasoning.](image2)

In terms of input characteristics, MMMU incorporates interleaved text and image inputs that require models to perform joint multimodal understanding and complex subject reasoning [4]. The benchmark features 30 heterogeneous visual formats, ranging from photographs, paintings, and chemical structures to medical images and sheet music, with structured technical visuals like diagrams (3,466) and tables (2,474) forming the largest share of the dataset [1].

![Diagrams and tables represent the largest proportion of visual formats present in the MMMU dataset.](image5)

In summary, MMMU advances beyond existing datasets by requiring college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning across six major academic disciplines, utilizing 11.5K questions with interleaved text-image inputs and 30 diverse visual formats dominated by technical diagrams and tables.

In disciplined agile project management, addressing changing stakeholder needs is recognized as a fundamental process goal, particularly during the Construction phase of the delivery lifecycle [2]. 

![Addressing changing stakeholder needs is highlighted as a core Construction goal within Disciplined Agile Delivery.](image2)

To fulfill this goal effectively, teams rely on continuous **Needs Exploration** while developing a consumable solution. Needs Exploration encompasses a range of practices that allow teams to discover and clarify requirements incrementally rather than attempting to define everything upfront. Key techniques within needs exploration include active stakeholder participation, Acceptance Test-Driven Development (ATDD), high-level and detailed requirements specifications, split (A/B) testing, Just-In-Time (JIT) model storming, and look-ahead modeling.

![Needs Exploration incorporates techniques such as active stakeholder participation, ATDD, and JIT model storming to continuously refine requirements.](image5)

Complementing needs exploration, specific **Elicitation Methods** serve as the practical techniques used to extract, discuss, and validate evolving stakeholder requirements. Essential elicitation strategies include JIT model storming, look-ahead modeling, iteration demos, and all-hands demos, which work best alongside active stakeholder participation.

![Elicitation methods such as JIT model storming, look-ahead modeling, and iteration demos help capture evolving stakeholder requirements.](image1)

Needs Exploration and Elicitation Methods contribute to addressing stakeholder needs by enabling agile teams to continuously discover, elicit, and validate requirements through iterative feedback, just-in-time modeling, and active stakeholder participation throughout the development lifecycle.

Racial identification among self-identified Hispanics varies significantly depending on generational status, showing a clear shift away from identifying racially as Hispanic or Latino toward identifying as White or Other across successive generations.

Among foreign-born Hispanics, the vast majority—78%—identify racially as Hispanic or Latino. Only 11% identify as White, 6% as Other, and 3% as Black. 

For second-generation Hispanics, the proportion identifying racially as Hispanic or Latino drops to 66%. Meanwhile, those identifying as White increases to 15%, and those selecting Other grows to 13%, with 2% identifying as Black.

This trend continues into the third or higher generation, where less than half (46%) identify racially as Hispanic or Latino. Conversely, 25% identify as White, 20% identify as Other, and 4% identify as Black.

![Across generations, self-identified Hispanics become less likely to identify racially as Hispanic or Latino and more likely to identify as White or Other.](image1)

In summary, foreign-born Hispanics predominantly identify racially as Hispanic or Latino, whereas later generations increasingly identify as White or Other as the percentage identifying racially as Hispanic or Latino declines.

The RAPTOR model consistently demonstrates superior performance across various benchmarks, datasets, and language processing metrics when compared to traditional retrieval methods like BM25 and DPR, as well as existing state-of-the-art architectures.

When evaluating general retrieval accuracy, RAPTOR achieves higher accuracy than BM25 and DPR under both GPT-3 and UnifiedQA model backbones.

![RAPTOR achieves the highest accuracy across both GPT-3 and UnifiedQA settings compared to BM25 and DPR.](image1)

On challenging benchmark datasets, RAPTOR paired with GPT-4 outperforms models such as Longformer-base, DPR with DeBERTaV3-large, and CoLISA, reaching an accuracy of 82.6% on the Test Set and 76.2% on the Hard Subset.

![RAPTOR paired with GPT-4 achieves the highest accuracy on both the Test Set and the Hard Subset.](image2)

Across downstream text generation and retrieval evaluations, integrating RAPTOR into standard retrieval systems (such as SBERT, BM25, and DPR) systematically boosts performance across ROUGE, BLEU-1, BLEU-4, and METEOR metrics.

![Augmenting SBERT, BM25, and DPR with RAPTOR yields consistent gains across ROUGE, BLEU-1, BLEU-4, and METEOR metrics.](image3)

On datasets requiring precise contextual answer matching, such as QuALITY and QASPER, RAPTOR-augmented retrievers consistently yield higher accuracy and answer F1 scores than their non-RAPTOR counterparts.

![RAPTOR integration improves Accuracy on QuALITY and Answer F1 on QASPER across SBERT, BM25, and DPR retrievers.](image4)

Specifically on the QASPER dataset, RAPTOR paired with GPT-4 sets a benchmark with a 55.7% F-1 score, outperforming CoLT5 XL's 53.9% [4]. Furthermore, when comparing retriever methods across GPT-3, GPT-4, and UnifiedQA, RAPTOR achieves the highest F-1 match score across all three backbones.

![RAPTOR achieves the highest F-1 Match scores across GPT-3, GPT-4, and UnifiedQA backbones compared to Title + Abstract, BM25, and DPR retrievers.](image5)

Finally, on the Narrative QA dataset, RAPTOR paired with UnifiedQA 3B outperforms BM25 and DPR by 7.3 and 2.7 points in ROUGE-L, while also leading across BLEU-1, BLEU-4, and METEOR metrics [1, 2]. By taking advantage of intermediate layers and tree-clustering approaches to capture general themes alongside specific details, RAPTOR outperforms previous recursive summarization systems across all metrics and establishes a new state-of-the-art score in METEOR [2, 3].

![RAPTOR paired with UnifiedQA achieves a state-of-the-art METEOR score on the Narrative QA dataset while outperforming prior baseline models.](image6)

Across diverse evaluation metrics and datasets including Narrative QA, QASPER, and QuALITY, RAPTOR consistently outperforms traditional retrievers and state-of-the-art baselines, setting top scores in accuracy, F1, and METEOR metrics.

Across multi-document reading comprehension tasks such as WIKIHOP and MEDHOP, BiDAF consistently outperforms FastQA [3]. Although both models perform nearly indistinguishably on single-hop QA datasets like SQuAD, BiDAF exhibits a distinct advantage in multi-document settings [3]. This advantage stems from BiDAF's architecture, which employs iterative conditioning and latent interactions across multiple layers, enabling it to better integrate information distributed across several documents [2, 3].

When evaluating across different datasets and evaluation setups:

- **Standard vs. Gold Chain Settings**: BiDAF achieves higher accuracy than FastQA across standard setups as well as gold chain conditions (where only the supporting chain of reasoning documents is provided) [3]. Under gold chain conditions, BiDAF (masked) reaches up to 81.2% (test) / 85.7% (test*) on WIKIHOP and up to 99.3% (test) / 100.0% (test*) on MEDHOP, whereas FastQA (masked) achieves 65.3% / 70.0% on WIKIHOP and 51.8% / 55.1% on MEDHOP.

![Performance comparison of BiDAF and FastQA under standard and gold chain settings on WikiHop and MedHop datasets](image2)

- **Cross-Document Inference & Document Removal**: When intermediate documents without candidate mentions are removed to test multi-step reasoning capabilities, BiDAF shows a performance drop across the board (e.g., dropping from 54.5 to 44.6 on WIKIHOP test), proving that it actively leverages cross-document contextual information [4]. FastQA, having fewer latent interactions, shows inconclusive performance shifts (such as a slight increase from 35.8 to 38.0 on WIKIHOP test), highlighting its limitations in effectively integrating cross-document information [4].

![Performance comparison showing the impact of removing non-candidate documents (rem) on BiDAF and FastQA on WIKIHOP and MEDHOP](image1)

BiDAF consistently outperforms FastQA across both WIKIHOP and MEDHOP datasets under standard, gold chain, and document-ablation conditions due to its superior capacity for cross-document information integration.

The monitor uses different combinations and states of blue and amber (or orange) LED lights to indicate its internal power and operational status [1]. 

![The table describes different modes indicated by the status of blue and amber lights, such as Power On, Searching for signal, Stand-by mode, and Power Off modes.](image1)

The specific meanings of the LED light combinations are:

* **Blue: ON, Amber: OFF**: The monitor is in **Power On Mode** and an image is actively being displayed [1].
* **Blue: ON, Amber: ON**: The system is currently **Searching for a signal**.
* **Blue: OFF, Amber: ON**: Either **No signal found** or the display is in **Stand-by mode**.
* **Blue: OFF, Amber: OFF**: The monitor is in **Soft Power Off Mode** (the soft power button was pressed) or **Hard Power Off Mode**, indicating no image is displayed and the monitor is not internally powered [3].
* **Flashing Orange**: If the indicator flashes orange, it signals an error state; you should count the number of flashes, turn off the power, and contact your dealer for support.

In summary, the LED light combinations inform you whether the monitor is powered on and displaying an image, searching for or missing an input signal, in standby or powered off mode, or encountering an operational issue.

SPECTER significantly outperforms SciBERT across a wide variety of downstream tasks, including document classification, user activity prediction, citation prediction, and paper recommendation [3]. Even when SciBERT is fine-tuned directly on task-specific supervision signals—such as co-views, co-reads, co-citations, or a multitask combination of these signals—SPECTER's fixed representations consistently achieve superior results without requiring any task-specific fine-tuning [1, 4].

![SPECTER achieves higher overall performance across classification, user activity, citation, and recommendation metrics compared to task-specific SciBERT fine-tuned variants.](image2)

Across broad benchmark comparisons, SPECTER consistently reaches higher metric scores (such as F1, MAP, and nDCG) than standard SciBERT and other baseline embeddings [3].

![SPECTER consistently outperforms standard SciBERT across classification, user activity prediction, citation prediction, and recommendation tasks.](image4)

Visualizing and analyzing the 2D projections of their document embeddings provides clear structural insights into why SPECTER achieves better performance [2].

![SPECTER produces noticeably tighter and more separated topic clusters than SciBERT in 2D projections.](image1)

SPECTER's embeddings encode topical information far more effectively than SciBERT, resulting in noticeably tighter and more distinct discipline clusters [2]. Additionally, SPECTER's embedding space naturally captures cross-topic relationships; related fields such as Engineering, Mathematics, and Computer Science cluster close to one another, while Business and Economics similarly lie in close proximity [2]. Quantitative clustering evaluations using DBScan support these visual observations: SPECTER achieves homogeneity and completeness scores of 0.41 and 0.72 respectively, compared to SciBERT's lower scores of 0.19 and 0.63, demonstrating a substantial improvement in topic separation [2].

SPECTER consistently outperforms SciBERT across all evaluated downstream tasks without needing fine-tuning while producing embedding spaces with significantly clearer topic separation and domain relationships.

In the benchmark settings for MedMNIST and CIFAR-10, the choice of data augmentation depends on the modality of the dataset [2].

In the proposed model architecture, the input consists of representations for the claim ($\mathbf{c}^{(i)}$), reason ($\mathbf{r}^{(i)}$), warrant zero ($\mathbf{w}_{0}^{(i)}$), and warrant one ($\mathbf{w}_{1}^{(i)}$) [2]. ![The model architecture computes logits for each argument-warrant pair and passes their concatenation through a Softmax layer to generate a final prediction.](image1)

Once the logits $z_{0}^{(i)}$ and $z_{1}^{(i)}$ are obtained, they are concatenated and passed through a specific function to determine a probability distribution over the two candidate warrants, defined as $\mathbf{p}^{(i)}\!\stackrel{\cdot}{=}\!\mathrm{softmax}\!\big([z_{0}^{(i)},z_{1}^{(i)}]\big)$ [1].

The function used to determine a probability distribution over the two warrants is the **softmax** function.

An Engine Control Unit (ECU)—also referred to as a powertrain control module (PCM) or engine control module (ECM)—is an embedded electronic system that acts as the primary controller for an internal combustion engine's electrical subsystems [1, 2]. 

At the center of an engine management system, the ECU serves as the main processing unit that continuously determines the precise amount of fuel, ignition timing, and other vital parameters needed to keep the engine running efficiently [1]. It accomplishes this by reading real-time values from multidimensional lookup maps and various diagnostic sensors [1].

![The Engine Control Unit acts as the central control hub, processing data from sensors to manage fuel injectors.](image1)

The ECU receives direct input from essential engine sensors, including the Engine Temperature Sensor, Intake Air Temperature Sensor, Mass Air Flow Sensor, Throttle Position Sensor, HEGO (Heated Exhaust Gas Oxygen) Sensor, Crankshaft Sensor, and Camshaft Sensor [image1]. By evaluating these sensor inputs [1], the ECU outputs precise control signals to actuate components such as individual cylinder injectors (e.g., Injectors 1 through 6) and cold start injectors [image1].

![The ECU processes data from various engine sensors to manage fuel delivery and system performance.](image2)

Specifically, the ECU fulfills several critical roles within the vehicle's engine management system:

- **Fuel Delivery and Regulation**: The ECU processes data received via the sensor harness to regulate fuel delivery, sending output signals across the injector harness to control how much fuel is sprayed into the cylinders [1, image2].
- **Ignition Timing Control**: For spark-ignition engines, the ECU adjusts the precise timing of the spark (ignition timing) to deliver better overall engine power and fuel economy [4].
- **Idle Speed Management**: Most engine systems integrate idle speed control directly into the ECU [3]. Using the crankshaft position sensor to monitor engine RPM, the ECU adjusts a programmable throttle stop or an idle air bypass control stepper motor to maintain a steady idle [3].

In summary, the role of the Engine Control Unit (ECU) is to process real-time data from engine sensors to dynamically regulate fuel injection, ignition timing, and idle speed for optimal engine performance and efficiency.

When repetition control is introduced into a model designed for question-asking, it noticeably reduces the overall frequency of question-asking in the generated text [1]. 

Specifically, while standard question-asking conditional training can increase question rates up to nearly $100\%$ at higher control levels (such as $z = 10$), adding repetition control drops the rate to $79.67\%$ at the same control level [1]. 

![Adding repetition control to question-controlled conditional training significantly reduces the percentage of generated utterances containing questions across control levels.](image1)

This reduction occurs because the repetition control mechanism (specifically features like `extrep bigram` during weighted decoding) discourages bigrams that have previously appeared in earlier utterances [1]. As a result, it prevents the model from generating bigrams that are frequently necessary to construct common questions, such as "do you" or "what is" [1].

In conclusion, introducing repetition control lowers the frequency of question-asking because it penalizes common bigrams that are essential for forming standard questions.

BHP's Nomination and Governance Committee ensures effective board succession planning and director development by overseeing board renewal, evaluating director performance, and maintaining continuous development programs [3]. Following the initial induction, Non-executive Directors participate in ongoing training overseen by the committee, which covers environmental, social, and governance (ESG) topics, as well as updates regarding BHP's assets, commodities, geographies, and markets [1]. Throughout the year, the Chair discusses specific development needs with individual Directors, tailoring learning opportunities to specific committee memberships and the Board's areas of focus [4].

![The Nomination and Governance Committee oversees succession planning, evaluation and training, and corporate governance practices at BHP.](image2)

To manage board succession planning and the appointment of new members, BHP follows a structured eight-step process:

1. **Rigorous approach**: A structured method is used to maintain a diverse pipeline of candidates, focusing on required skills, tenure, experience, and risk management capabilities.
2. **Continuous approach**: Succession planning operates continuously using a nine-year tenure guideline to maintain a balance between experienced perspectives and fresh viewpoints.
3. **Role description**: The Nomination and Governance Committee outlines specific criteria and attributes for new positions based on governance standards.
4. **Selection and appointment of search firm**: An external search firm is engaged to conduct a global search matching the defined role description.
5. **Board interviews**: Shortlisted candidates are reviewed by the Chair and the committee, followed by meetings with every Board member.
6. **Committee recommendation**: The Nomination and Governance Committee recommends the preferred candidate to the Board.
7. **Background checks**: Thorough background and reference checks are performed with the assistance of external consultants.
8. **Letter of appointment**: Formal letters of appointment and written agreements detailing role definitions, independence, and terms are provided to the candidate.

![BHP utilizes an eight-step process to manage Board succession planning and the appointment of new Non-executive Directors.](image1)

In conclusion, BHP's Nomination and Governance Committee ensures effective board succession and director development through continuous tailored training, regular performance reviews, and a structured eight-step recruitment framework.

Machine translation (MT) systems are significantly prone to gender-biased translation errors [1], consistently achieving higher translation accuracy when presented with stereotypical gender roles compared to non-stereotypical ones across various target languages [1].

![Google Translate achieves higher accuracy for stereotypical gender translations across all tested languages compared to non-stereotypical ones.](image1)

To test whether gender bias can be influenced or corrected, stereotype-based adjustments can be introduced into the source text by prepending gendered adjectives—such as "pretty" for female entities and "handsome" for male entities—to nouns [4]. This creates mixed signals where the gendered adjective counteracts the system's default stereotypical profession bias [4]. For example, in Spanish, adding "pretty" shifts a biased male translation ("el panadero") to the correct female inflection ("la panadera bonita") when referring to a female baker [4].

![An example showing how prepending the adjective 'pretty' corrects a gender translation bias from male to female in Spanish.](image3)

These stereotype-based adjustments consistently increase translation performance and reduce bias across multiple target languages [4]. Experimental results demonstrate clear accuracy gains when adding these gendered adjectives (`+Adj`) [4].

![A table depicting significant accuracy improvements when adding gendered adjectives to source text in Spanish, Russian, and Ukrainian.](image6)

In conclusion, stereotype-based adjective adjustments provide strong gender cues that counteract profession biases, resulting in significant accuracy improvements and reduced gender bias across languages such as Spanish, Russian, and Ukrainian.

The transition from business intelligence (BI) to business analytics (BA) significantly elevates an organization's analytical capabilities by moving up the spectrum of intelligence and business value. 

![Business Intelligence and Business Analytics represent a continuum where moving to analytics increases both business value and the degree of intelligence.](image1)

In terms of data handling, business intelligence relies on descriptive, backward-looking reporting mechanisms like standard reports, ad-hoc queries, and alerts. At this baseline level, data handling is limited to converting raw data into structured information. When transitioning to business analytics, data handling evolves from simply processing raw data into information to combining both data and information to yield deep, actionable insights.

![Reporting converts data into basic information to raise questions, whereas Analysis synthesizes data and information into insights to answer questions.](image3)

Regarding insights generation, business intelligence primarily focuses on descriptive questions aimed at identifying "What happened?" or "Where exactly is the problem?", effectively raising questions without providing deeper answers. In contrast, business analytics shifts to a prescriptive and forward-looking orientation. By employing advanced techniques such as statistical analysis, forecasting, predictive modeling, and optimization, business analytics actively answers key strategic questions—explaining why events occur, predicting future outcomes, and determining the optimal actions to take.

In conclusion, transitioning from business intelligence to business analytics enhances data handling by synthesizing data and information into actionable insights and advances insight generation from identifying historical issues to providing predictive, forward-looking solutions.

The hyperparameter $\alpha$ in the Tversky Index plays a significant role in manipulating the tradeoff between false-negatives and false-positives, causing the F1 score performance to vary noticeably as $\alpha$ changes across different datasets [1]. 

![The table presents F1 score performance across different alpha values for the Chinese Onto4.0 and English QuoRef datasets.](image1)

As shown in the experimental evaluations across values of $\alpha$ ranging from 0.1 to 0.9:

- For the **Chinese Onto4.0** dataset, the F1 score begins at 80.13 (for $\alpha = 0.1$), increases steadily to reach its peak, and subsequently declines to 80.21 as $\alpha$ approaches 0.9 [1].
- For the **English QuoRef** dataset, a similar trend is observed: the F1 score starts at 63.23 (for $\alpha = 0.1$), peaks, and then falls to 64.84 when $\alpha = 0.9$ [1].

An ideal defense against text attacks aims to balance low sensitivity with a low word error rate (WER); however, achieving a lower error rate often comes at the expense of higher sensitivity [1]. The trade-offs associated with different backoff strategies—such as Pass-through, Background, and Neutral—vary substantially between closed vocabulary (word-only) and open vocabulary (char-only, word+char, word-piece) models [4].

For **closed vocabulary models**, downstream word-only classifiers internally treat all out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words alike [4]. As a result, sensitivity remains tightly bounded within a narrow range (approximately 11.4 to 12.6) regardless of the backoff variant:
- **Pass-through** and **Neutral** backoffs perform identically in terms of error and sensitivity, yielding a WER of around 11.0 and sensitivity around 12.0.
- **Background** backoff achieves a slightly lower WER of ~10.5, though it incurs a slightly higher sensitivity of ~12.7 ![The scatter plot for word-only models shows that sensitivity remains tightly bounded around 11.4 to 12.6 across all backoff variants, with Background achieving the lowest WER.](image1).

For **open vocabulary models**, downstream classifiers process every unique combination of characters differently, causing sensitivity to fluctuate dramatically across backoff strategies (ranging from ~10 to 30) [4]:
- **Pass-through** backoff suffers from extremely high sensitivity (~30) alongside a WER near 10, providing weaker overall defense [4].
- **Background** backoff substantially improves word recognition by drawing from a larger corpus, reducing WER to ~7.0 and lowering sensitivity to ~10.0 [2], [3].
- **Neutral** backoff maps `UNK` predictions to a fixed neutral word, limiting the number of unique predicted outputs and successfully keeping sensitivity low (~12) at a slightly higher WER (~11) [3], [4] ![The scatter plot for char-only models shows severe sensitivity spikes under Pass-through backoff compared to the significantly lower sensitivity of Neutral and Background variants.](image1).

In summary, closed vocabulary models maintain relatively constant sensitivity across backoff strategies with minor WER differences, whereas open vocabulary models exhibit severe sensitivity spikes under Pass-through backoff that are effectively reduced by Background and Neutral strategies.

In evaluating navigation and manipulation task execution across the LANI and CHAI datasets, the **'Our Approach'** method consistently outperforms baseline models as well as previous state-of-the-art approaches like MISRA17 and CHAPLOT18 [4]. 

On the **LANI** navigation task, 'Our Approach' achieves a lower Stop Distance (SD) of 8.43 and the highest Task Completion (TC) rate of 36.9% [4], improving task completion accuracy by approximately 5% over CHAPLOT18 while significantly outperforming MISRA17 [4]. On the more challenging **CHAI** dataset, where previous approaches fail to learn effectively, 'Our Approach' maintains superior performance, achieving an SD of 3.34 and a Manipulation Accuracy (MA) of 39.97% [4].

![The table presents comparative results showing that Our Approach achieves the best performance across both LANI and CHAI datasets in terms of SD, TC, and MA.](image2)

### Key Factors Influencing Performance

Several structural and environment-specific factors influence these results:

1. **Decomposed Architecture**: A major contributor to the performance gain is the decomposition of goal prediction and action generation [3]. Rather than generating immediate step actions, the neural network processes text instructions alongside panoramic visual features to first form a goal probability map to pinpoint the target location, which then guides action selection [3].

![Diagram illustrating the neural network architecture that processes text and vision inputs to predict goal probability distributions before outputting actions.](image6)

2. **Linguistic Ambiguity and Human Benchmark Gap**: Inherent ambiguities in natural language instructions make exact target identification difficult [1, 3]. Human evaluation benchmarks achieve an SD of 5.2 and TC of 63% on LANI, and an SD of 1.34 with 100% MA on CHAI [1]. This reveals that while 'Our Approach' advances current automated techniques, a large performance gap remains relative to human capabilities [1, 3].

3. **Task Complexity Differences**: Performance across all models is weaker on CHAI compared to LANI, primarily due to the intricate manipulation requirements and overall higher task complexity present in CHAI [3, 4].

In summary, 'Our Approach' achieves superior Stop Distance and Task Completion rates over baseline and prior methods on both LANI and CHAI by decoupling goal prediction from action planning, though overall performance remains constrained by linguistic ambiguities and task complexity relative to human capability.

Throughout the coronavirus pandemic, partisan divides have played a far greater role in shaping public opinion on policy effectiveness and the causes of virus spread than the actual local health impact experienced by individuals [1]. Geographic differences in virus severity are largely overshadowed by political affiliation [2]. For instance, a clear majority of Democrats (80%) attribute rising case numbers to an increase in actual infections, whereas most Republicans (62%) view expanded testing as the main driver for higher case counts `![Perceptions of whether rising COVID-19 cases are driven by more testing or new infections are strongly split by political affiliation.](image5)`.

These political divisions strongly influence how Americans evaluate response measures and policy priorities. Democrats overwhelmingly cite inadequate federal government responses (82%), premature lifting of restrictions (82%), and insufficient mask-wearing or social distancing (89%) as major reasons for the virus's spread, while far fewer Republicans share these concerns `![Democrats and Republicans hold vastly different views on the factors contributing to the spread of COVID-19, including federal response and compliance with safety measures.](image2)`. Political orientation also dictates views on economic recovery; Democrats consistently hold higher agreement across all county conditions that suppressing infections to a comfortable level is essential to reopening the economy `![Partisan divides strongly influence views on COVID-19 recovery strategies and causes of case surges regardless of local death rates.](image1)`.

Regarding trust in institutions and leadership, partisan divides create deep contrasts, with one notable exception. Positive perceptions of local hospitals and medical centers cross party lines, earning high confidence from both Republicans (90%) and Democrats (87%) [4]. 

![Confidence in local hospitals is high across party lines, whereas trust in public health officials and political figures is deeply divided.](image3)

In contrast, trust in leadership and public health institutions remains highly polarized [4]. Public health officials like those at the CDC command greater trust among Democrats (72%) than Republicans (53%), while trust in political figures such as Donald Trump reveals an extreme divide—73% among Republicans compared to just 6% among Democrats `![Confidence in local hospitals is high across party lines, whereas trust in public health officials and political figures is deeply divided.](image3)`.

In conclusion, partisan divides heavily polarize views on COVID-19 response effectiveness, the causes of virus spread, and trust in public officials, while local medical institutions stand out as a rare point of bipartisan consensus.

Mobile internet users in Indonesia exhibit distinct demographic traits that heavily align with their digital content preferences, directly driving significant business opportunities in mobile advertising, digital entertainment, and e-commerce.

### Demographic Profile of Users
Mobile internet adoption in Indonesia is strongly skewed toward a young, male, and economically active population. Mobile users are predominantly male (71% male vs. 29% female) ![Gender distribution and ad impression growth in Indonesia](image2). In terms of age, 65% of mobile users are under 35 years old—specifically 32% between ages 18–24 and 33% between ages 25–35 ![Age distribution and occupation profile of internet users in Indonesia](image1). Occupationally, 39% of users hold full-time jobs, and nearly one-fourth (32% combined) are businessmen or entrepreneurs, alongside 12% who are students ![Age distribution and occupation profile of internet users in Indonesia](image1).

### Mobile Content Preferences
This young and active demographic uses mobile internet primarily for communication, media consumption, and entertainment:
- **Primary Activities**: Social media occupies the largest share of mobile internet activity at 24%, followed by entertainment (20%), general information (16%), and email (14%) ![Breakdown of mobile internet activities and downloaded content](image3).
- **Downloaded Content**: Downloads are heavily dominated by games and apps (70%), video (49%), and music (44%) ![Breakdown of mobile internet activities and downloaded content](image3). 
- **Information & Social Media Engagement**: Social media penetration is exceptionally high, with 92% of Indonesian internet users owning a Facebook account, nearly 90% of whom access it via mobile devices [1]. Furthermore, 60% of internet users rely on online channels as their main source of information ahead of traditional news media [1].

### Potential Business Opportunities
These demographic characteristics and consumption habits translate into major commercial potential across several areas:

1. **Mobile Advertising & Brand Engagement**: Mobile devices are the top influencer in customer decision-making at 55%, outranking television (49%) and desktop PCs (39%) [3]. Reflecting this shift, mobile ad impressions in Indonesia expanded dramatically from 8.2 billion in Q1 2013 to over 16.3 billion in Q1 2014 ![Gender distribution and ad impression growth in Indonesia](image2), making Indonesia the 2nd largest market after the US for InMobi mobile ads [1].
2. **Digital Entertainment & Gaming Monetization**: The overwhelming user preference for downloading games/apps (70%), video (49%), and music (44%) creates strong opportunities for mobile gaming studios, content creators, streaming platforms, and app developers ![Breakdown of mobile internet activities and downloaded content](image3).
3. **Targeted Mobile Commerce & Services**: Because nearly one-fourth of mobile internet users are entrepreneurs or businessmen and 39% work full-time ![Age distribution and occupation profile of internet users in Indonesia](image1), there is substantial commercial scope for mobile shopping platforms, productivity apps, and location-based service (LBS) advertising [3].

In summary, the young, predominantly male, and working-class demographic of Indonesian mobile internet users drives strong engagement with mobile social media, gaming, and video content, creating lucrative business opportunities in mobile advertising, digital entertainment, and mobile commerce.

As claims increase in reasoning complexity from 2-hop to 4-hop scenarios in the HOVER dataset, both the nature of model errors and overall performance undergo distinct shifts.

To analyze error distributions, human evaluation of prediction failures categorizes errors into syntactic errors, semantic errors (token, structure, subtask), and incorrect execution [4]. 

![The distribution of error types reveals that syntax errors are 0%, semantic errors increase with hop count to 77% in 4-hop claims, while execution errors dominate simpler 2-hop and 3-hop claims.](image1)

Syntax errors remain at 0% across all reasoning hops, indicating that program generation models maintain valid grammar regardless of claim complexity. However, semantic errors rise sharply from 29% in 2-hop claims to 38% in 3-hop claims, peaking at 77% in 4-hop claims. This sharp growth in semantic errors for 4-hop claims is largely driven by program structure mistakes, which jump to 57%. In contrast, incorrect execution errors—where the generated program is correct but fails during execution—predominate in lower-hop claims (71% in 2-hop and 62% in 3-hop) before decreasing to 23% in 4-hop claims.

Regarding model performance, increased claim complexity leads to noticeable drops in accuracy across models [3]. For example, the F1 score of DeBERTaV3-NLI drops by 21.7% from 77.22 on 2-hop claims down to 60.49 on 4-hop claims [3]. Methods utilizing explicit program-guided reasoning (such as ProgramFC) suffer much smaller performance degradations (a 11.7% drop) [3]. Furthermore, step-by-step reasoning strategies like Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting perform better as reasoning hops increase compared to direct prompting [1].

![F1 scores across model sizes show ProgramFC continuously outperforming FLAN-T5 across 2-hop, 3-hop, and 4-hop HOVER tasks.](image3)

Model scaling consistently benefits performance across all complexity levels, with ProgramFC maintaining superior F1 scores over baseline models like FLAN-T5 across all model sizes (from 80M to 11B parameters) on 2-hop, 3-hop, and 4-hop HOVER tasks.

![Retrieval recall comparison highlights that ProgramFC consistently achieves higher recall than one-step retrieval across all HOVER hop settings and FEVEROUS-S.](image5)

Similarly, retrieval recall decreases as the number of required hops grows; for example, one-step retrieval drops from 73.18 on 2-hop claims to 36.43 on 4-hop claims. However, ProgramFC consistently outperforms single-step retrieval across all HOVER hop levels (77.13% on 2-hop, 59.17% on 3-hop, 49.93% on 4-hop) as well as on the FEVEROUS-S dataset (85.65% vs 76.25%).

As reasoning hops increase from 2-hop to 4-hop, overall model accuracy and retrieval recall decrease while semantic and structural program errors rise significantly over execution errors, though program-guided models like ProgramFC remain consistently superior across HOVER hops and FEVEROUS datasets.

When comparing the SWEM and CNN models across various subspace dimensions and text classification datasets, distinct patterns emerge regarding parameter efficiency, peak accuracy, and sensitivity to feature structures.

At low subspace dimensions, SWEM exhibits significantly higher accuracy than CNN, demonstrating that SWEM is far more parameter-efficient for acquiring a strong baseline solution [3]. For instance, on datasets like AG News, SWEM achieves an $80\%$ testing accuracy threshold at a much lower intrinsic dimension ($d_{\mathrm{int}}$) compared to CNN [3]. As the subspace dimension increases, both models show accuracy improvements that gradually approach their full-capacity baselines [3].

![As the subspace dimension increases, the accuracy of both SWEM and CNN models improves, with SWEM showing higher parameter efficiency at lower dimensions.](image2)

However, when the subspace dimension $d$ becomes large, CNN is able to leverage its additional trainable parameters to achieve higher accuracy [3]. This advantage is particularly visible on datasets like Yelp Polarity, where CNN outperforms SWEM as capacity grows [3]. Across broader benchmarks—such as AG News, Yahoo! Answers, and DBpedia—SWEM variants (like SWEM-concat) remain highly competitive, often reaching top-level performance that matches or exceeds various CNN architectures [3]. 

![SWEM variants demonstrate competitive or superior performance compared to CNNs on several benchmark datasets like AG News and DBpedia.](image3)

In sentiment analysis tasks where sequence structure is critical, CNNs generally maintain a performance edge because their compositional structure captures spatial and word-order information, which standard SWEM models lack [1, 2].

In summary, SWEM is more parameter-efficient and achieves superior accuracy at lower subspace dimensions, whereas CNN attains higher overall accuracy at higher dimensions and on complex sentiment tasks by using trainable parameters to capture word-order information.

In adversarial learning strategies such as DSGAN, the performance of the discriminator on the distant-supervision negative set $N^D$ serves as a benchmark to assess the learning progress of the generator [1, 2]. Initially, the discriminator achieves high accuracy because the generator has not yet acquired the capability to generate challenging samples [1, 2]. However, as training progresses across epochs, the generator learns to produce more accurate true positive samples in each bag, causing the discriminator's accuracy on $N^D$ to gradually drop [2].

![The line graph illustrates the discriminator's accuracy on $N^D$ over epochs, showing that for /people/person/place_lived (red curve with square markers), the accuracy decreases steeply from near 1 and levels off slightly below 0.75.](image1)

For the relation type `/people/person/place_lived` (represented by the red curve with square markers), the accuracy starts near 1.0 at early epochs and undergoes a steep decline before reaching its critical stabilization point slightly below 0.75 around epoch 35 to 45, at which point the accuracy no longer decreases significantly.

In the context of **"Conscious Incompetence"**, as the number of absent knowledge elements increases:

- **Recall** remains stable at around 15 regardless of the amount of missing knowledge [1].
- **Precision** exhibits a significant upward trend (rising from around 14 to about 26) [1].
- **F1-Score** shows a moderate upward trend [1].

![The line graph demonstrates that in the conscious incompetence experiment, precision and F1-Score increase while recall stays stable as knowledge elements are removed.](image2)

These trends imply that current large language models (LLMs) have a limited ability to identify absent knowledge [1]. However, as the knowledge graph coverage problem worsens, explicitly marking absent knowledge (e.g., using `[NA]`) enables the model to locate missing knowledge more accurately, making the "Conscious Incompetence" setting increasingly crucial [1].

Conversely, in **retrieval analysis**, when required knowledge is removed or retrieval accuracy drops:

- Both **precision** and **recall** fall drastically [2].
- The negative impact is significantly greater on **recall** than on **precision**, with recall dropping in a nearly linear fashion [3].

![The retrieval analysis line graph shows that precision, recall, and F1-score all decline as retrieval accuracy decreases.](image3)

These changes demonstrate that while LLMs possess some ability to filter out incorrect knowledge—mitigating the drop in precision—a lack of provided knowledge severely impairs citation quality because a model cannot cite knowledge that is not retrieved [2, 3].

In summary, while LLMs can maintain a steady ability to identify and locate absent knowledge when prompted for conscious incompetence, removing necessary knowledge during retrieval severely reduces their overall citation precision and recall.

As the number of demonstration samples $K$ increases from 1 to 5, there is a distinct and noticeable improvement in Micro-F1 performance across both the MAVEN-ERE and Causal-TimeBank (CTB) datasets [2, 3]. However, when further increasing the number of demonstration samples beyond this point (e.g., to 10 or 20), subsequent gains in Micro-F1 performance become diminishing and limited [3].

![The graph illustrates that Micro-F1 scores increase significantly from 1 to 5 demonstrations and plateau at higher counts, while logical constraints consistently elevate overall performance across all sample sizes.](image1)

Throughout all tested demonstration sample sizes, incorporating logical constraints provides stable and clear performance enhancements [3]. Notably, adding logical constraints to prompts with fewer demonstrations can even outperform configurations that use a larger number of demonstrations without logical constraints [3]. For example, on the MAVEN-ERE dataset, using 5 demonstration samples with logical constraints reaches a Micro-F1 score of 25.7%, which surpasses the 24.5% Micro-F1 score obtained using 10 demonstrations without logical constraints [3].

In conclusion, increasing demonstration samples from 1 to 5 substantially boosts Micro-F1 performance before plateauing at higher counts, while adding logical constraints consistently enhances performance across all sample sizes, allowing smaller demonstration sets with constraints to outperform larger sets without them.

Users' comfort level with social media companies using their personal data heavily depends on the specific purpose of that data usage [3]. Across all age demographics, people are generally comfortable with platforms utilizing data to suggest local activities, but remain deeply wary when that same data is applied to political messaging [1, 2]. 

![Acceptability of social media data usage varies significantly by age and purpose, with local event recommendations receiving the highest support and political campaign ads receiving the lowest.](image1)

When examining specific uses, recommending local events garners broad acceptance across every age category [1]. For instance, 80% of users aged 30 to 49 and 78% of users aged 18 to 29 consider local event recommendations acceptable, compared to 72% of those aged 50 to 64 and 67% of users aged 65 and older [1]. 

However, clear age gaps emerge regarding other algorithms, as older users are markedly less comfortable with social media platforms using their data for personal connections or targeted commercial advertising [4]. A solid two-to-one majority of younger adults aged 18 to 49 (66% for ages 18–29 and 67% for ages 30–49) find friend recommendations acceptable, whereas a 63% majority of adults aged 65 and older view this practice as unacceptable, with only 36% expressing approval [4]. Similarly, while 60% of adults aged 30 to 49 find targeted product and service ads acceptable, acceptance drops to just 39% among users aged 65 and older [4]. In contrast, political campaign messaging suffers low acceptance across all age brackets, peaking at just 40% among ages 30 to 49 and dropping to 31% for ages 65+ [1]. 

Overall, while younger age groups generally exhibit higher acceptance toward data usage for friend suggestions and product ads than older adults, user comfort across all age groups remains highest for local event recommendations and lowest for political campaign messaging.

Baseline CLIP models typically exhibit a precision gradation tied to class frequencies, where performance progressively increases from rare categories ($AP_r$) through common ($AP_c$) to frequent categories ($AP_f$) [3]. In contrast, integrating the Retrieval-Augmented Reranking (RAR) mechanism into multimodal large language models (MLLMs) alters this performance trend [3]. RAR models achieve peak precision on rare categories ($AP_r$), surpassing baseline CLIP models by as much as 19.6 percentage points due to effective contextual retrieval from external memory and reranking for lesser-represented classes [3].

![The table highlights that RAR models consistently outperform baseline CLIP models across AP metrics, with RAR (InternLM-XC2) achieving the largest gains.](image1)

When evaluating precision across category metrics ($AP_r$, $AP_c$, $AP_f$, and $AP_{all}$), RAR-integrated MLLMs—including LLaVA1.5, Qwen-VL, and InternLM-XC2—demonstrate comprehensive accuracy improvements over baseline CLIP variants, with RAR (InternLM-XC2) delivering the highest gains across most metrics.

![The table displays object detection improvements of RAR variants over the CLIP baseline across different scale AP metrics.](image3)

Similarly, across various object scales in detection metrics ($AP_s$, $AP_m$, $AP_l$, and $AP_{all}$), RAR model variants consistently beat the baseline `CLIP w/ box` model, achieving superior precision scores overall.

In summary, RAR models consistently outperform baseline CLIP models across all average precision metrics, showing particularly large improvements in rare class precision ($AP_r$) and object detection performance across scales.

The author divides the multi-step reasoning process of causal inference—termed the Causal Chain-of-Thought (CausalCoT) framework—into **6 key steps** structured across two distinct phases [1], [3]:

* **Step 1: Extract/Identify the Causal Graph** — Identifying the variables and the causal graph structure $\mathcal{G}$ [1], [3].
* **Step 2: Determine/Classify the Query Type** — Identifying the specific type of causal question (e.g., Average Treatment Effect) [1], [3].
* **Step 3: Formalize the Query** — Expressing the query precisely in formal symbolic notation [1], [3].
* **Step 4: Collect Available Data** — Extracting all relevant statistical and quantitative data from the prompt [1], [3].

![An illustrative scenario demonstrating the 6 sequential reasoning steps for addressing a causal question.](image2)

### 2. Solution Phase (Steps 5–6)
* **Step 5: Derive the Estimand** — Deducing the mathematical estimand using formal causal inference techniques such as do-calculus and probability basics [1], [3].
* **Step 6: Solve for the Estimand** — Plugging the collected data into the estimand formula and performing arithmetic calculations to yield the final answer [1], [3].

The author divided causal inference into 6 key steps.

The workshop structures its learning objectives into three distinct modules [2]:

In Module 1 (Basic), participants learn how to construct basic flat, clustered, and layered maps directly in Wikidata using geo-referenced (P625) items and SPARQL queries [1].

![Module 1 focuses on creating basic flat and layered maps in Wikidata using SPARQL queries and geo-referenced items.](image3)

In Module 2 (Intermediate), the focus shifts to learning how to embed these Wikidata-driven maps into other Wikimedia platforms, including Wikipedia and Wikimedia Commons [1]. 

In Module 3 (Advanced), learners focus on creating interactive, layered Wikidata-driven maps designed for off-Wiki usage within standard HTML web pages [1].

![Learning objectives across three modules highlight progressing from basic Wikidata SPARQL queries to embedding maps in Wikimedia sites and creating interactive off-Wiki maps.](image1)

To support these objectives, participants are equipped with tools such as SPARQL, OpenStreetMap, GeoJSON, the MediaWiki Kartographer extension, basic Python, and Jupyter Notebooks [1]. Additionally, learning resources such as SPARQL query examples, Python code snippets, and adaptable template materials are provided to allow participants to build maps using their own datasets [4].

In conclusion, the workshop guides learners through creating Wikidata maps, embedding them across Wikimedia projects, and developing interactive off-Wiki maps using SPARQL, OpenStreetMap, GeoJSON, Kartographer, Python, Jupyter, and reusable code snippets.

In a standard single-task model (Figure 1a), the architecture consists of a single decoder that relies on a single attention mechanism to attend to the hidden states generated by the encoder [3]. 

In contrast, the multitask model represented in Figure 1b jointly models two separate output sequences using a shared encoder [4]. In terms of decoder attention, instead of relying on a single attention mechanism, the multitask model equips each of its two separate decoders with its own independent attention mechanism, enabling both decoders to separately attend to the states of the shared encoder `![The single-task model utilizes one decoder with a single attention mechanism, while the multitask model uses two decoders, each with its own separate attention mechanism attending to a shared encoder.](image1)`.

Unlike the single-task model which has only one attention mechanism for its single decoder, the multitask model uses two separate attention mechanisms, allowing each of its two decoders to independently attend to the shared encoder states.

The Translation Ranking model processes its input through a specific pipeline designed to optimize sentence embeddings based on relative translation quality [1, 3]. 

According to Figure 2, the model receives an input tuple $\chi = (s, h^+, h^-, r)$ comprising four distinct segments: the source text ($s$), the reference translation ($r$), a higher-ranked ("better") hypothesis ($h^+$), and a lower-ranked ("worse") hypothesis ($h^-$) [1, 2]. 

![The diagram illustrates the sentence embedding process through a pretrained encoder, pooling layer, and triplet margin loss optimization.](image4)

Each of these four segments is passed independently through a pre-trained cross-lingual encoder followed by a pooling layer to aggregate features and generate a dense sentence embedding for each segment [1, 2]. 

Once sentence embeddings for $\{s, h^+, h^-, r\}$ are produced, the architecture computes the triplet margin loss [1, 2]. This optimization objective minimizes the distance in the embedding space between the "better" hypothesis ($h^+$) and the anchor representations (both the original source $s$ and reference $r$), while separating the "worse" hypothesis ($h^-$) from them [1, 3].

In summary, the Translation Ranking model independently encodes four input segments—source, reference, better hypothesis, and worse hypothesis—through a pre-trained encoder and pooling layer, then uses triplet margin loss to minimize the embedding distance between the better hypothesis and the source/reference anchors.

Perceptions regarding whether Islam encourages violence are closely divided among the American public, with $46\%$ believing Islam is more likely than other religions to encourage violence among its believers and $45\%$ believing it is not [1, 4]. While overall public views on this issue have remained relatively stable over time [2], tracking from 2002 to 2015 shows a notable shift toward a more divided sentiment ![A line graph tracking public perception from 2002 to 2015 on whether Islam is more likely to encourage violence compared to other religions.](image1).

This division is clearly mirrored in concern over Islamic extremism, where Republicans consistently express much higher levels of concern both globally and within the United States than Democrats or Independents ![Line graphs illustrating political affiliation differences in concern about Islamic extremism worldwide and in the U.S. from 2007 to 2015.](image5).

These partisan perceptions strongly relate to views on how the government should handle the threat of terrorism. Republicans, who express greater concern over religious violence and extremism, overwhelmingly believe government measures are "Not tough enough" ($84\%$) ![A table outlining survey responses across political groups regarding whether anti-terrorism approaches are sufficiently tough.](image2) and strongly advocate that military force is the best way to defeat terrorism ($72\%$) ![A bar chart detailing agreement across political affiliations on using military force to combat terrorism.](image3). Conversely, Democrats are far less inclined toward military intervention, with $66\%$ arguing that an over-reliance on military force creates more hatred and terrorism ![A bar chart detailing agreement across political affiliations on using military force to combat terrorism.](image3).
